analysis.one_liner: Repeals the ACA requirement that large employers offer health coverage or pay a fee.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Health Subcommittee on May 5 and 11, 2011, and died there at the end of the 112th Congress, despite 213 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike the Affordable Care Act's employer mandate from the tax code, ending the rule that employers with 50 or more full-time workers must offer health coverage or pay a penalty, and removing the related reporting requirements [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Boustany and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, then its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup or vote [S1] [S5]. Although 213 representatives cosponsored it, the House never took it up [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, employers with 50+ employees — especially low-wage chains that lean on the exemption — would have been freed from paying the $2,000-per-worker penalty and from the Section 6056 reporting paperwork [S3]. Large restaurant, retail, and hospitality employers (franchise chains like McDonald's, Yum!, and Darden) had lobbied hard for exactly this relief and would have been the main beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the tax penalty under section 4980H that applies to employers with 50 or more full-time employees who do not provide coverage [S2] [S3].
It eliminates the Section 6056 information-reporting requirements the ACA imposed on large employers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, employees at large firms who would lose offers of coverage would pay, through higher premiums or out-of-pocket costs in the individual market; taxpayers and other insured people would also absorb the cost, since repealing the employer mandate worsens the ACA's risk pool.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the employer mandate means some large employers would drop coverage, pushing workers into the individual market with higher premiums and fewer protections, and worsening the ACA risk pool.
Repealing Section 6056 reporting would remove the data the IRS needs to verify coverage and enforce the individual mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes almost entirely to large employers — savings on penalties and paperwork. The cost is borne diffusely by workers, taxpayers, and other premium payers, which is why the bill is hard to defend as a good deal overall.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee referred it to its Health Subcommittee on May 11, 2011, and it never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died there when the 112th Congress ended [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Introduced May 5, 2011 by Rep. Boustany with two original cosponsors [S1] [S5].
Referred to House Ways and Means on May 5; referred to the Health Subcommittee on May 11 [S1] [S5].
Never reported out of subcommittee or given a floor vote; ended the Congress without action [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one got a legislative win. Workers kept employer coverage protected by the ACA mandate in the short run. The fight moved to the regulatory arena, where the employer mandate was later delayed — an outcome low-wage employers scored as a win without needing this bill to pass [S2] [S5]. ,

for.name: Rep. Charles Boustany (R-LA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: Restaurant, retail, and franchise chains
for.what_they_did: Publicly lobbied to delay or repeal the employer mandate, citing cost and paperwork burdens.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or vote; it died there.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled enough seats to block or heavily resist full repeal of a signature ACA provision; none of the 213 cosponsors were more than 3 Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican: 210 of 213 cosponsors were Republicans, with only 3 Democratic cosponsors [S4]. Congress.gov does not record any vote or committee action on the bill beyond the May 5 and May 11 referrals, so the partisan split on a hypothetical roll call is not directly observable — but the 210-to-3 cosponsor ratio is strong evidence that the bill was a Republican priority with almost no Democratic support [S1] [S4]., },

industries.note: The bill would have spared them the $2,000-per-worker penalty for not covering employees and eliminated Section 6056 reporting paperwork — a direct transfer of cost away from the employer. Workers at these firms would have borne the cost in reduced coverage and higher premiums.
Losing employer-mandate coverage would shrink enrollment from large-group plans, but firms that dropped coverage would shift workers to individual-market plans, partially offsetting the loss.
Repealing the mandate eliminates penalty revenue that would have helped fund ACA coverage subsidies.
